vulnerabilities.title: ConnectWise ScreenConnect MSP Console Hijacking and the 'SCKit' Toolkit: Huntress Totals Are Reported Today as 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organisations - Lower Than This Feed Recorded Yesterday - the RMM+ Extension Accepted a Blank Access Key, and the Root Cause Is Still Not Established
affected_products: ConnectWise ScreenConnect - cloud-hosted instances (primary observed target)
ScreenConnect 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783 (both observed affected - running the latest release was not protective)
On-premises ScreenConnect deployments running any of the five 'RMM+' family extensions
Downstream: every endpoint managed by a compromised MSP's ScreenConnect instance
vulnerabilities.summary:
A second correction, and a more precise picture of the mechanism.

On the numbers: yesterday's run recorded a second wave on 13 November adding 205 hosts across 41 organisations and a running Huntress total past 490 endpoints and 89 organisations. Today's reporting consistently puts the Huntress figure at at least 288 endpoints across 48 Huntress-protected organisations, with earlier counts of 286 endpoints across 47 organisations and six compromised MSPs. The lower figure is the one carried today because it is what multiple current sources say; it is possible the higher number reflected a later update not reproduced in today's results, and that possibility is recorded rather than resolved. Either way the figure is one vendor's customer visibility and is not a global count.

On the mechanism, which is now clearer and is the useful part. Huntress began seeing the activity at around 17:47 UTC on 11 November. Attackers used ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to install an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client plus the SCKit toolkit onto customer machines, and all observed infections occurred within about 90 minutes. Huntress attributes the deployments to commands issued through management consoles rather than to verified autonomous spread, even though SCKit contains self-propagation logic - so calling it a worm overstates what has been observed. The link to RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension, is the strongest lead: Huntress says RMM+ bypasses ScreenConnect user accounts, roles and MFA, and reporting states that RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 accepted a blank access key where an administrator had never configured one. ConnectWise identified approximately 400 partner environments with at least one listed extension and disabled the extensions where it could act - that 400 is an exposure count, not a victim count, and the two should never be added together.

What is still unknown. ConnectWise reports no evidence of a compromise of its own infrastructure and no evidence that initial access involved a ScreenConnect vulnerability; the client flaw SCKit targets was patched in September. Huntress's telemetry points at compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions but it has not confirmed how the attackers got in. No actor has been named and no ransomware has been tied to this wave. Microsoft's Security Blog published its own analysis of SCKit on 13 November.

Why it stays in a UK-focused list. The same argument as entry 8: a hijacked MSP console is administrative access to every customer behind it, and the UK public sector's long tail - districts, parishes, academies, GP federations, small charities holding public data - is administered through exactly these platforms. If your IT is delivered by an MSP, the question to ask in writing today is whether RMM+ or any third-party ScreenConnect extension was installed in the environment that manages you, and whether ConnectWise contacted them as one of the ~400.

Confidence is medium. All figures are from secondary coverage of Huntress and ConnectWise; huntress.com, connectwise.com and the Microsoft Security Blog were not reachable in this environment, and today's totals contradict yesterday's.
recommended_actions: RE-CHECK EVEN IF YOU CHECKED MIDWEEK: a second wave on 13 November added 205 hosts across 41 organisations after ConnectWise had already disabled RMM+ and four other extensions. That means the route is not demonstrably closed, and an assessment completed on Wednesday no longer covers you.

Today: ask every MSP and IT outsourcer with remote access to your estate, in writing, whether they run ConnectWise ScreenConnect, whether their instance is cloud-hosted, and whether any 'RMM+' family extension was installed. Treat a non-answer as a yes and isolate accordingly.

In on-premises ScreenConnect deployments, disable the RMM+ family extensions immediately - ConnectWise has already disabled them in ~400 cloud environments but on-premises operators must act themselves.

Do NOT triage a suspected infected endpoint over ScreenConnect. Use out-of-band access (EDR live response, direct console, separate RMM) - connecting through the compromised tool exposes the responder's workstation.

Hunt for the full set of ScreenConnect clients installed across your estate and reconcile against the authorised instance identifier; a second, unauthorised client is the campaign's persistence mechanism.

Hunt for Microsoft Defender exclusion additions created in the last 7 days, especially any created by a process parented to a ScreenConnect service - this preceded payload staging in the observed intrusions.
Hunt for any process executed as SYSTEM with a ScreenConnect service as the parent, concentrating on the 11 November 17:00-20:00 UTC window and the following 72 hours.
Rotate credentials, API keys and session tokens that any ScreenConnect-managed endpoint could reach, and force re-authentication for privileged accounts used by support technicians.
Obtain and ingest the Huntress and ConnectWise indicator lists directly - they were published with the research and are more current than any relayed summary.
Review and restrict ScreenConnect's 'Run command' capability by role; it is the execution primitive that turned console access into SYSTEM on 288 machines.

Reconcile every installed ScreenConnect client against your authorised instance identifier again, including on endpoints you cleared last week, and hunt for Defender exclusions added in the last three weeks.

If your provider uses ScreenConnect, ask specifically whether it was in either wave, whether RMM+ or any other third-party extension was installed, and whether any technician workstation has been examined - Microsoft's analysis describes the toolkit as built to reach technician sessions.

kql.name: Burst of SYSTEM-context command execution under the ScreenConnect client (both waves)
kql.description: Untested. Targets the mechanism rather than any payload: mass Run Command abuse appears as many endpoints executing shell commands under the ScreenConnect service within minutes of each other. Covers 11-14 November 2026 to catch both waves; widen if your provider's estate was affected later.
kql.query:
let WaveStart = datetime(2026-11-11T00:00:00Z);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp >= WaveStart
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwisecontrol", "connectwise")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "certutil.exe", "curl.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| summarize Executions = count(), Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by bin(Timestamp, 15m), DeviceName, AccountName
| order by Timestamp asc, Executions desc

kql.name: Technician-workstation exposure check: ScreenConnect client activity on IT-support endpoints
kql.description: Untested. Inverts the usual direction of travel. Microsoft describes the toolkit as designed to reach technician sessions, so run this against the IT-support and MSP-administrator device group specifically and look for anything that is not an outbound support session.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where tolower(FileName) has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwisecontrol") or tolower(ProcessCommandLine) has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwisecontrol", "&e=access&", "instanceid")
| summarize Events = count(), Commands = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| order by Events desc

kql.name: Process executed by ScreenConnect service as SYSTEM (SCKit staging)
kql.description: Untested. Core detection: the operators used ScreenConnect's native Run command to execute as SYSTEM. Baseline your MSP's legitimate scripted activity first, then alert on anything outside it.
kql.query:
let SCProcs = dynamic(["screenconnect.clientservice.exe", "screenconnect.windowsclient.exe", "connectwisecontrol.clientservice.exe", "screenconnect.service.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (SCProcs)
| where AccountName in~ ("system", "nt authority\\system")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "msiexec.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Microsoft Defender exclusion added (SCKit pre-staging)
kql.description: Untested. Installation scripts added Defender exclusions before deploying payloads. Any exclusion added by a remote-management parent is high-signal; exclusions are rare and deliberate in most estates.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference", "ExclusionPath", "ExclusionProcess", "ExclusionExtension", "MpCmdRun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Exclusion", "DisableRealtimeMonitoring", "DisableIOAVProtection")
| extend ViaRemoteTool = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise"), "YES", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ViaRemoteTool, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by ViaRemoteTool desc, Timestamp desc

kql.name: Second / unauthorised ScreenConnect client installed
kql.description: Untested. The campaign installed a rogue ScreenConnect client alongside the legitimate one for redundant access. Replace the AuthorisedInstance string with your own instance identifier to make this precise.
kql.query:
let AuthorisedInstance = "REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-INSTANCE-ID";
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect.Client", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient", "ConnectWiseControl.Client", "ScreenConnect.ClientSetup")
   or FolderPath has_any ("ScreenConnect Client", "ConnectWise Control Client")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| extend Unexpected = iff(FolderPath has AuthorisedInstance, "expected", "REVIEW")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Unexpected, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Unexpected asc, Timestamp desc

kql.name: Burst detection - same command across many endpoints in a short window
kql.description: Untested. All observed infections occurred inside 90 minutes. This surfaces the pattern itself: one command line executing across an unusual number of distinct devices in a short period, which is how mass push via a hijacked console looks in telemetry.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise")
| summarize DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceName), Devices = make_set(DeviceName, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by ProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 90m)
| where DeviceCount >= 5
| extend SpreadMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| project Timestamp, DeviceCount, SpreadMinutes, FirstSeen, LastSeen, ProcessCommandLine, Devices
| order by DeviceCount desc

kql.name: ScreenConnect client beaconing to an unexpected relay
kql.description: Untested. A rogue client calls home to the attacker's relay, not yours. Add your legitimate relay FQDN(s) to the allowlist; everything else from a ScreenConnect process warrants investigation.
kql.query:
let KnownRelays = dynamic(["REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-RELAY.screenconnect.com", "REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-RELAY.hostedrmm.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) or isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| extend Host = tolower(coalesce(RemoteUrl, RemoteIP))
| where not (Host has_any (KnownRelays))
| summarize Connections = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by Host, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemotePort
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.summary:
The UK corporate picture as at the morning of 16 November 2026. One new GB-tagged leak-site listing appeared inside the window, and the two items most likely to matter to a UK government reader are not it.

NEW INSIDE THE WINDOW. A leak-site aggregator recorded on 16 November 2026 that an entity listed as CARRINGTON, country code GB, has been claimed by the Vortex ransomware operation, with a stated deadline of 19 November 2026. Vortex is flagged by the aggregator as a new group, with roughly 14 victims in total and recent listings including KOCH in Germany on the same day and Scripps, Arthrex, Karlstorz and Pyramid Healthcare on 10 November, several of them with large claimed exfiltration volumes. Confidence in this listing is low: 'CARRINGTON' is not resolved to a specific company in any source located, no victim statement exists, and emerging operations have a documented record of mis-tagged and fabricated claims. It is recorded as a lead, not a breach, and it should not be reported internally as a confirmed UK incident.

THE ONE WITH CONFIRMED SUBSTANCE: RATHBONES. Citywire reported on 9 November that sensitive client data was accessed in a cyber attack on Rathbones, the wealth manager with roughly GBP 121 billion under management. Rathbones has contacted affected clients, required all staff to complete virtual cyber security training, and posted scam warnings on its client portal; its shares dipped around 2 per cent and partly recovered. What is not known is as striking as what is: no categories of affected data have been disclosed, it has not been established whether data was copied, altered, deleted or misused, no entry vector has been published, and no threat actor has been linked to it. This is a confirmed access to sensitive financial client data at a major UK institution with essentially no technical detail in the public domain, and the scam warnings on the client portal are the tell that the firm expects follow-on fraud against its clients. A leak-site aggregator recorded on 12 November that INC Ransom has listed Computacenter, naming Pivot Technology Solutions and Sigma Solutions - the North American IT services businesses the UK group acquired - with an estimated attack date of 4 November. Sources disagree on whether the exposure is the UK parent or only the US units, and Computacenter has not publicly confirmed an incident. The reason it is in a UK government feed regardless is that Computacenter is one of the larger suppliers of IT infrastructure, hardware and managed services to UK public bodies. Even a US-scoped incident at a group of that shape is a supplier-assurance question for any department, council or trust with a live contract - and the question to ask is narrow: was any system holding our data, credentials or access in scope. INC Ransom's leak site shows 34 UK victims in total with its most recent post on 9 November.

Confidence is low to medium and varies by item: Rathbones is medium (press-confirmed with company actions on the record), Computacenter and Fittleworth are low (unverified leak-site claims), and CARRINGTON is low and additionally unresolved as to identity. No leak-site page, company statement or ICO record was retrieved directly - ransomware.live and the news sites were not reachable in this environment.
recommended_actions: UK professional services firms: read the SilentRansomGroup / Luna Moth pattern rather than the single A&O Shearman listing. The group exfiltrates data through social engineering rather than encrypting, so there is no outage to notice - which means your detection has to be identity and data-egress telemetry, and your help desk is the attack surface.

If you are a 118 118 Money customer organisation or hold a relationship with any entity named here, check for a notification you may have filed as marketing: the company has notified the ICO and is offering twelve months of fraud monitoring, which indicates identity-usable data was taken.

If your organisation, a subsidiary or a named supplier appears in these listings, treat it as a live incident until disproved: preserve logs immediately, engage incident response, and assess ICO notification obligations against the 72-hour clock from awareness.

Monitor extortion leak sites for your own brands, trading names, acquired entities and key suppliers daily rather than relying on being told - all but one of these victims learned of it from the listing.

Audit acquired and legacy systems specifically. The Maersk case is a legacy system inherited through acquisition; run a discovery exercise for estates that never completed onboarding into monitoring, patching and identity governance.

Map your professional-services supply chain - legal, accountancy, payroll, recruitment - and confirm each firm's breach-notification commitments. The A&O Shearman listing is a reminder that privileged client data concentrates in these firms.

For UK mid-market organisations without 24/7 monitoring, prioritise the basics these groups rely on: MFA on all remote access, no internet-exposed RDP, offline or immutable backups with a tested restore, and EDR on servers as well as workstations.
Rehearse the extortion decision before you face it: who authorises contact, who speaks publicly, what your position on payment is, and what your ICO and law-enforcement reporting path looks like.
Report incidents to the NCSC and Action Fraud; the NCSC Annual Review's incident figures depend on reporting and under-reporting degrades the national picture that UK defenders rely on.
Do not act on an unverified leak-site listing as though it were confirmed when communicating externally - verify first, then communicate, to avoid amplifying a fabricated claim.

Verify the nationality of any aggregator-tagged 'UK' listing before escalating it: this run found a GB-tagged 'camden-living' entry that resolves to a US multifamily residential operator, and the one new listing in the window (K&A Industries, Interlock, 13 November) states no country at all. Country tags on leak-site aggregators are the most common source of false UK positives.

Maersk contract-logistics customers: ask specifically whether your data sat in the LF Logistics / OCF platform inherited through the 2022 acquisition, which is the system Maersk has confirmed as the scope of its incident.

Record every listing in this entry at its stated confidence level. Apart from Maersk's confirmation and the 118 118 Money notifications these are unverified criminal claims, and the most common failure mode with this entry is a low-confidence listing being cited internally a fortnight later as an established breach.

kql.name: Pre-extortion reconnaissance - impossible travel and legacy authentication
kql.description: Untested. Listings lag intrusion by weeks (16 October to 12 November for bristol-companies). This looks back far enough to cover that lag, focusing on legacy auth and geographic anomalies.
kql.query:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where ClientAppUsed in ("IMAP4", "POP3", "SMTP", "Other clients", "Exchange ActiveSync", "Authenticated SMTP")
   or RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("medium", "high")
| summarize SignIns = count(), Countries = make_set(Location, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 30), Apps = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 10) by UserPrincipalName
| where array_length(Countries) > 1
| order by SignIns desc

kql.name: Mass file access and staging consistent with pre-encryption exfiltration
kql.description: Untested. Detects the collection stage that precedes both encryption and leak-site listing. Tune the threshold to your environment; backup and indexing services will need exclusion.
kql.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("backup.exe", "veeam.backup.manager.exe", "SearchIndexer.exe", "OneDrive.exe", "MsMpEng.exe"))
| summarize FileCount = count(), Folders = dcount(FolderPath), Extensions = make_set(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]), 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where FileCount > 2000
| order by FileCount desc

kql.name: Large outbound transfers to file-sharing and cloud-storage services
kql.description: Untested. Exfiltration to commodity file-sharing services is the normal precursor to a leak-site listing. Review volume per destination rather than per connection.
kql.query:
let ExfilHosts = dynamic(["mega.nz", "mega.io", "anonfiles", "gofile.io", "file.io", "transfer.sh", "wetransfer", "dropbox", "pcloud", "mediafire", "temp.sh", "bashupload", "catbox.moe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (ExfilHosts)
| summarize Connections = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceName), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Connections desc

kql.name: Backup and shadow-copy destruction (pre-encryption impact preparation)
kql.description: Untested. High-fidelity late-stage detection. Any hit should be treated as an active incident, not a hunting lead.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vssadmin delete shadows", "wbadmin delete", "bcdedit /set", "recoveryenabled no", "wmic shadowcopy delete", "Delete-VMSnapshot", "Remove-VMSnapshot", "catalog quiet")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

summary_statistics.highest_priority_action: Five things, and the first two are inventory questions rather than patches - which is the shape of this whole run. (1) ANSWER THE REFRIGERATION AND BUILDING-SERVICES QUESTION TODAY, because the UK government said today that it is working with affected organisations and the next thing that happens is somebody asks you for your position. How many refrigeration, HVAC and building-management controllers do you own, which have a management interface reachable from the internet, and who maintains them. Do not trust the asset register - query Shodan or Censys against your own ranges and your sites' separate DSL and 4G lines, because these devices are typically connected by an engineer on a circuit IT does not know exists. Then remove public management access via VPN, private APN or a firewall allowlist. That single control answers ranks 1, 2 and 3 at once, and it is the only control that works for the Danfoss AK-SM800A, where six pre-authentication RCEs have no patch, no CVEs and no scanner signature, and for Copeland XWEB EVO units that reached end of software support in March 2026. For NHS, pharmacy, pathology and research cold storage, add one step: make sure a temperature excursion procedure can distinguish a commanded setpoint change from a plant fault, because the loss in this campaign is the destroyed batch, not the controller. (2) PATCH SONICWALL SSLVPN BEFORE FRIDAY AND THEN CHECK WHETHER YOU WERE ALREADY USED. CVE-2026-19868 is a confirmed-exploited SAML and MFA bypass - SonicOS 7.3.4-7013 or 8.2.3-8015, no workaround, KEV due 20 November. It scores only 7.1, which is why it has been under-triaged everywhere, and what it actually does is make MFA stop applying to remote access with no visible configuration change. SonicWall has published no indicators and no compromise check, so the test is yours: reconcile 45 days of successful SSLVPN sessions against SAML assertions at your identity provider and treat any session with no matching assertion as a compromised account. Audit the local, LDAP and RADIUS fallback accounts left behind by the SAML migration while you are there - those are the credentials the flaw needs. (3) TWO KEV DEADLINES FALL TODAY. Check Point CVE-2026-123039, the Gaia DynamicCLI root escalation, is being exploited against a couple of dozen customers in a chain that starts at the Mobile Access portal and has ended in a wiper on ESXi hosts - and it carries mandatory forensic triage under BOD 26-04, so patching alone does not discharge it. UnrealIRCd CVE-2026-114713 is due today as well. Chrome CVE-2026-125350 and Outlook CVE-2026-124194 are due on the 24th and reach every desk in government. (4) UPDATE XEN ORCHESTRA AND DO NOT TRUST ITS LOGS. VSA-2026-062 is actively exploited, needs no authentication, gives Admin on the management plane and root on XCP-ng hosts, has no CVE - so no scanner will raise it - and Vates states that successful exploitation leaves no log of the unauthenticated access. Update to 6.9.2 or 6.10.1, take the interface off any network it does not need, rotate every credential and token the appliance holds, and verify that your backups are not sitting inside the pool they protect. (5) ASK YOUR MSP TWO PRECISE QUESTIONS IN WRITING, and note that both entries behind this are softer today than this feed reported yesterday. For N-able: is the Legacy API enabled on the server that manages us, and what hotfix level are we on - an MSP that says the Legacy API has always been disabled has given a genuinely reassuring answer. For ConnectWise ScreenConnect: was RMM+ or any third-party extension installed in the environment that manages us, at what version, and did ConnectWise contact you as one of the approximately 400 partner environments. Separately, if you hold a live Computacenter contract, ask whether any system holding your data, credentials or access was in scope of the incident INC Ransom has claimed.
